title: Nodal Lines
concept: A square plate whose sand lines reshape as two equal-pitch modes trade weight, stepping up through four mode pairs.

mechanism_embodied.mechanism_name: Degenerate mode pair on a square plate
mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: The shader evaluates cos(n pi x)cos(m pi y) + s cos(m pi x)cos(n pi y) on a square and paints a sand-coloured band where the value is near zero. The weight s drifts continuously, and every five seconds the mode pair crossfades to the next of (1,3), (2,5), (3,7), (4,9).

discarded_obvious_idea: A particle simulation of sand bouncing on a plate was discarded: it needs thousands of particles, does not fit 4 KB comfortably, and the result is grainy noise before it settles.
motion_sound_plan: No sound. The mixing weight oscillates slowly so the lines keep moving; the mode pair advances on a fixed five-second step with a one-second crossfade. Under prefers-reduced-motion the clock runs at one fifth speed.

storyboard.description: Mode pair (1,3): a few broad sand loops on a grey plate, slowly bending as the weight drifts.
Crossfade to (2,5): the loops split into a denser lattice of rounded cells.
Crossfade to (3,7): more cells, lines pinch into X-shaped crossings.
(4,9): the densest figure, still drifting, held to the end.

memorable_moment: The moment a set of loops pinches into crossing lines as the weight passes through zero.
self_declared_risk: In the densest mode pairs the fwidth-based line width may shimmer or alias on the software renderer as the weight drifts.
liner_note: Chladni bowed sand-covered plates in 1787 and drew where the sand came to rest. The sand gathers on nodal lines, the parts of the plate that do not move. On a square plate two modes can share a pitch, and the figure you see depends on how they mix. This piece draws the zero line of that mix, cos(n pi x)cos(m pi y) plus a weighted swap of n and m, and slowly changes the weight. Every five seconds it moves to a higher mode pair, so the lines multiply. Explaining these figures was the subject of the Paris Academy prize that Sophie Germain won in 1816.
